content:
Hope Taylor Swift won't feel troubled by this news, but a doctoral student in entomology at the University of California, Riverside has recently named a new genus of plant-eating insects discovered in Australia after the singer.

Sarah Schroeder has just co-published a paper in the journal 'Insect Systematics and Evolution' that describes 12 new insect species, including a genus she named after Taylor Swift herself — Swiftiephylus.

The genus Swiftiephylus contains four species, all with Latin names inspired by Taylor Swift and her albums: Swiftiephylus taylorae, Swiftiephylus amator, Swiftiephylus intrepidus, and Swiftiephylus poetorum.

Schroeder pointed out that these bugs bear a slight resemblance to her favourite celebrity.

"Taylor Swift's signature look is blonde hair with red lips. These insects are pale yellow, dotted with red markings," Schroeder said in a University of California, Riverside press release. "In the paper I refer to them as 'blondes.'"

HuffPost reached out to Taylor Swift, but she has not yet responded to this new bug-related honour. Schroeder, however, hopes the singer's star power can shine on these insects to "raise awareness about the undiscovered diversity of insects."

Although Schroeder and her co-author, UC Riverside professor of entomology Christiane Weirauch, are credited as the species' namers, the insects were actually collected between 1995 and 2004.

Schroeder hopes that naming a genus after Swift will raise public awareness of the importance of taxonomy.

"If we don't go out and describe species, we won't know they exist and we won't be able to protect them," she said. "Naming these species after Taylor is a way of paying tribute to her, but also a tribute to conservation science, and a way to draw attention to all the unknown diversity that's still out there."

It seems these Taylor Swift bugs will not bring negative effects to the singer: they are not known to cause pest problems for humans or animals, nor do they harm the host plants on which they spend most of their time.

These Australian bugs are not the first insects to be named after Swift.

Back in 2022, a brown-orange millipede discovered in the forests of Tennessee was named Nannaria swiftae by a Taylor Swift fan scientist.
